Re-smooth the next-state probabilities of a fitted tree

Source: R/smoothing.R
smooth_tree.Rd

smooth_tree() re-estimates the next-state probabilities of every context of a fitted tree under a new smoothing scheme, without refitting. Smoothing moves part of the probability toward unobserved states or toward the distribution of the shorter context, the parent in the tree (Chen & Goodman, 1999). The next-state distribution of a context is estimated from the continuations observed after it; raw proportions give probability zero to every continuation that was not observed, which makes any new sequence containing such a continuation impossible under the model, and they are unstable in contexts with few occurrences.

Counts and the set of contexts stay as they are, and only the probabilities change. Parents are smoothed before their children, so the back-off schemes interpolate with an already smoothed parent. The five schemes are given under Details. It returns a tree of the same class with re-smoothed probabilities.

Smoothing changes predictions, perplexity and the divergence column of tree_pathways(), but never which contexts the tree contains; that is set by min_count and by pruning. To compare schemes on one dataset use compare_smoothing() (in-sample) or tune_tree() (cross-validated).

Usage

smooth_tree(tree, smoothing = "floor")

Arguments

tree

A transitiontrees object, or a transitiontrees_group, whose trees are each re-smoothed.

smoothing

A method name, or a list of the method name and its hyperparameters, such as list("kneser_ney", discount = 0.5). Methods and default hyperparameters: "floor" (default; ymin = 0.001, rule = "interpolate"), "laplace" (alpha = 1), "kneser_ney" (discount = 0.75), "witten_bell" (none) and "jelinek_mercer" (lambda = 0.5).

Value

An object of the same class as tree with re-smoothed probabilities; counts and contexts are unchanged.

Details

For a context with counts \(n_s\) over \(k\) states, total \(n\) and parent distribution \(q_s\) (uniform for the root):

"floor"

With rule = "interpolate" (default), a distribution with an unobserved state becomes \((1 - k\,y_{min}) p_s + y_{min}\), so that each unobserved state has probability exactly ymin; distributions without zeros are left unchanged. ymin must be below \(1/k\). With rule = "cap", every probability is raised to at least ymin and the vector is renormalized.

"laplace"

Additive smoothing: \((n_s + \alpha) / (n + k\alpha)\).

"kneser_ney"

Absolute discounting with back-off to the parent: \(\max(n_s - d, 0)/n\) plus the removed mass times \(q_s\). The parent's smoothed distribution is used for the back-off, not the continuation counts of the original method (Kneser & Ney, 1995).

"witten_bell"

Interpolation with the parent, \((1 - \lambda) n_s / n + \lambda q_s\), with \(\lambda = r / (r + n)\) and \(r\) the number of distinct states observed after the context (Witten & Bell, 1991).

"jelinek_mercer"

Interpolation with the parent at a fixed weight: \((1 - \lambda) n_s / n + \lambda q_s\).

Conditions

transitiontrees_bad_input when tree is not a fitted tree, the method is unknown, a hyperparameter is outside its range, or ymin is not below \(1/k\) under rule = "interpolate".

References

Begleiter, R., El-Yaniv, R., & Yona, G. (2004). On prediction using variable order Markov models. Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, 22, 385-421. doi:10.1613/jair.1491

Chen, S. F., & Goodman, J. (1999). An empirical study of smoothing techniques for language modeling. Computer Speech and Language, 13(4), 359-393. doi:10.1006/csla.1999.0128

Kneser, R., & Ney, H. (1995). Improved backing-off for M-gram language modeling. In 1995 International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing (Vol. 1, pp. 181-184). doi:10.1109/ICASSP.1995.479394

Witten, I. H., & Bell, T. C. (1991). The zero-frequency problem: Estimating the probabilities of novel events in adaptive text compression. IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 37(4), 1085-1094. doi:10.1109/18.87000

See also

compare_smoothing() to compare schemes; context_tree(), whose smoothing argument applies a scheme at fit time; tune_tree().

Examples

tree <- context_tree(trajectories, max_depth = 3)
smooth_tree(tree, "kneser_ney")
#> <transitiontrees>  38 nodes, depth <= 3, 3 states  [unpruned]
#>   alphabet : Active, Average, Disengaged
